ideas.idea: The textbook itself concedes that under uncertainty planning and control move toward the point of implementation, so the quarrel is with the playbook as practised, not the textbook.
ideas.note: F cites domain vs goal planning by level

ideas.idea: The textbook's own rule is that the more complex the change, the more employees must be involved; top-down Kotter-style change fits only predictable change.
The textbook model assumes a predictable, controllable world, while high-hazard traditions treat uncertainty and friction as permanent.
ideas.note: MCDP side supported; the textbook is not as uniformly deterministic as claimed

ideas.idea: Precise central control over events is infeasible under friction and uncertainty; the most a leader can impose is a general framework, and excessive control slows tempo.
A cascaded target handed down without its purpose goes stale when conditions change, leaving people chasing a number that no longer serves anything.
ideas.note: task obsolete, intent lasting; applied to KPIs

ideas.idea: Attach a purpose to every cascaded target ('task in order to purpose') and let the purpose govern when the target goes stale.
Mission tactics: prescribe method only as far as coordination needs, and have subordinates act and inform rather than wait for permission.
People should understand the intent two levels up; test whether people two levels down can state it.
Information technology and live dashboards tempt seniors to keep precise, positive control over subordinates.
The further ahead a plan looks, the less precision it should try to impose.
Designate a single main effort to concentrate resources instead of spreading effort across many metrics.
ideas.note: contrast with balanced scorecard is the answers' application

ideas.idea: Cascades and approval routes through committees slow response, as mid-level leaders wait for sign-off instead of adapting.
ideas.note: general MCDP point applied; J's 'massive lag' is a strength the source doesn't carry

ideas.idea: Specific, difficult targets do raise performance (goal planning, Weyerhaeuser's 94% load target).
Keep plain targets for stable, repeatable work; the contradictions bite on uncertain work.
A schedule date became the yardstick programmes were judged by, and schedule pressure accumulated risk little by little without anyone deciding to trade safety.
Past success becomes justification: anomalies get normalised one acceptance at a time (normalisation of deviance).
Hitting the target, or a run of good quarters, is not evidence the risk is absent; the dangerous quarter is the one hit despite a warning sign.
ideas.note: applied from CAIB past-success finding and DOE 'bald tire'

ideas.idea: In quarterly reviews ask what deviation you got away with or what nearly went wrong, not only whether the target was hit.
ideas.note: follows from near-miss learning and normalisation findings

ideas.idea: Grading units with charts and statistics stifles discussion; a review should not grade success or failure.
Keep the KPIs but stop grading people with them in the room where you most need the truth.
ideas.note: follows directly from the AAR grading warning

ideas.idea: Things are counted because they can be; results are lagging indicators; measure what matters, not what is easy.
Production behaviours naturally win over prevention behaviours unless leaders hold up a strong culture; supervisors reward results and stay silent on safe behaviour.
Ask of every target what people will stop doing to hit it, and track that hidden cost.
ideas.note: follows from production-over-prevention premise

ideas.idea: Columbia does not condemn targets: aggressive schedules can signal a healthy institution, but their pressure on other goals must be watched.
Where status is missing, numbers are the great equaliser: data lets a voice without rank be weighed.
Separate the owners of cost and schedule from an independent authority over technical, quality or safety requirements who can say stop.
Judge people's behaviour and decisions on what was known at the time, not on outcomes; outcome-based judgement is shortsighted (performance = behaviour + results).
Performance is produced by the system: errors are symptoms of organisational conditions, so ask how the organisation failed the individual.
Most event causes and unsafe acts are organisational, not individual (85% of causes; ~90% of unsafe acts blameless; 81% of errors latent).
ideas.note: L's 'over 90% organisationally induced' stretches the figures

ideas.idea: Retraining people for slips is futile and insulting; no counselling or training changes human fallibility.
Blame and punishment drive mistakes and near misses underground; a just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture.
Put a written firewall between learning reviews and appraisal or discipline.
Apply a substitution test (would comparable peers have done the same?) before blaming an individual.
Redefine accountability as giving an honest account, with the organisation accountable for learning about and fixing conditions.
The textbook itself records the retreat from appraisal orthodoxy (GE dropping forced ranking; Deloitte's 58% of executives doubting performance management).
Deal leniently with errors of overboldness (no zero-defects mentality) and severely with inaction and timidity.
An outcome-scored review punishes the bold miss and rewards the safe non-attempt; reviews should ask whether someone ducked a decision that was theirs.
ideas.note: follows directly from MCDP's leniency/severity rule

ideas.idea: The traditions split on acting under uncertainty: MCDP's any decision beats none and boldness versus DOE/CAIB's prove-it-safe-before-proceeding and procedural rigour.
Resolve the split by sorting decisions or functions: bold and fast where mistakes can be undone, prove-it-safe where they cannot.
ideas.note: answers' own reconciliation; CAIB's centralise/decentralise hallmark is the nearest premise

ideas.idea: Columbia names the ability to run centralised or decentralised as each situation needs as the hallmark of a high-reliability organisation.
The traditions split on what the organisation is for: DOE makes safe work the overriding priority; the Forest Service says the agency does not exist to be safe.
The traditions split on causes: DOE (and CAIB's recommendations) keep root-cause analysis; the Forest Service bars causal statements and uses networked causality.
Post-incident recommendations and new rules add complexity that can increase risk, and leaders jump to action plans believing the problem solved.
Structural changes that make the organisation more complex create new ways to fail, and error risk rises while change beds in.
Audit the change programme for added process: count action items that added steps against those that removed one, and stop adding a committee per lesson.
ideas.note: follows loosely from LFUO and CAIB complexity warnings

ideas.idea: Use root-cause analysis for process or equipment failures and patterns, and condition reconstruction for judgement calls or single incidents.
ideas.note: answers' reconciliation of the RCA dispute

ideas.idea: Investigations that stop at the active human error leave latent causes in place; 'inattention to detail' is not a root cause.
New rules from a review should be created with, and vetted by, the people who do the work.
The traditions disagree on how blameless to be: NHS and DOE decision trees keep discipline; the Forest Service sets the bar at reckless, wilful disregard; the Marines punish timidity and yes-men.
The traditions disagree on retraining: the Army retrains to standard routinely; DOE calls retraining for slips an insult; the Forest Service lists forced retraining as discipline.

The traditions disagree on the status of rules: Army and DOE judge against standards and compliance; the Forest Service says experience teaches which rules get shortcut and judging by broken rules misses context.
The traditions disagree on oversight: Columbia wants centralised independent technical authority; MCDP wants decentralised command.
Information is rolled up and simplified as it rises, weak signals drop out, and the steering committee hears a filtered, green story.
Consensus sign-off verified by everyone's signature renders no one accountable; give each decision one named owner.
Leaders facing unanimous agreement should argue the other side and seek dissent; missing dissent is a warning sign.
NASA inverted the burden of proof, making engineers prove danger; requiring the front line to prove risk silences warnings.
Ask green status reports and forecasts to 'prove to me this has not been harmed'.
The steering committee's job should be hunting bad news; judge the change programme by whether bad news reaches it faster.
ideas.note: CAIB carries seeking dissent and filtered signals; the bad-news-speed measure is added

ideas.idea: DOE itself puts the senior team on a human performance steering committee, so the committee form is not the problem.
ideas.note: E frames it as a tension with learning reviews

ideas.idea: Leaders create culture and own changing it, so the work sits with the executive team, not the change programme.
Reviews rarely examine the decisions of those who commissioned them; put the executive team's own calls inside the review.
Allegiance to hierarchy, procedure and proper channels displaced deference to technical expertise; defer to the people closest to the work.
Find the gap between work as imagined by managers and work as actually done.
Replace top-down critiques and post-mortems with rank-free after-action reviews that compare intended with actual and do not grade.
Juniors owe honest disagreement before a decision and full support after; yes-men are not tolerated.
Believing you already have a strong safety culture is itself the blind spot.
Replacing or fixing the nearest person does not solve organisational problems and breeds a false belief that the problem is solved.
Reforms fade: the post-Challenger changes were undone over time by management actions.
Linear interventions in a system with feedback loops and delays produce counter-intuitive side effects; map the loops before launching change.
ideas.note: the term 'policy resistance' is not in the library

ideas.idea: Frontline intuition (MCDP) conflicts with systems thinking's finding that intuition fails on feedback and accumulation; intuition for tactics, mapping for structural design.
ideas.note: the split of roles is E's own

ideas.idea: Repurpose the steering committee solely to fund and fix the systemic traps that reviews surface, not to police behaviour.
At around 300 people the textbook machinery starts to grind: executives lose line of sight and middle layers filter information.
ideas.note: no source discusses company size thresholds

ideas.idea: Functional or capability silos optimise resource utilisation and breed handoffs and local optimisation; build complete cross-functional teams.
Cascading narrow output targets drives local optimisation; align units around customer outcomes instead.
ideas.note: Org Topologies carries output vs outcome, not goal cascading

ideas.idea: Independent technical authority conflicts with Agile's flat self-managing teams without internal hierarchy.
ideas.note: both premises present; the opposition is L's

ideas.idea: Fixed sprints conflict with continuous flow, which Kanban and Reinertsen say avoids the batching that timeboxes impose (Little's Law).
ideas.note: Open Kanban carries batch size; no anti-timebox claim or Little's Law

ideas.idea: Limit executive-level work in progress: fewer active initiatives and smaller batches speed feedback.
ideas.note: general point applied to executive initiatives

ideas.idea: The Forest Service's reluctance to issue recommendations may be impractical when a decision is needed by Friday.
